Senior executives ask hard questions every day, but the best ones rarely sound blunt. The secret is in the first few words. Compare two questions. When will the system be ready? And: could you tell me when the system will be ready? The information is the same, but the second question is softer, because it asks permission first. Notice also that the word order changes. After could you tell me, or do you know, the question becomes a normal sentence: when the system will be ready, not when will the system be ready. My second tip: never put someone on the spot in front of their boss. If the topic is sensitive, ask privately first. You can say: I was wondering if we could talk after the meeting. And my last tip: being tactful is not the same as being vague. You can be polite and still be candid. Ask the hard question, but open the door gently.

Hi Carlos, Tom Reyes here, from finance at Brightline. Thanks for your email on Thursday. I appreciated the tactful way you asked about the budget. To answer your first question, the cost overrun on the payroll bridge is about two hundred thousand dollars, mostly because of extra testing. I know that is a sensitive number, so I would rather present it to the committee myself. I was wondering if you could help me prepare the slides. And I have a question for you, too. Could you tell me who on your side will own the bridge after it goes live? Do you know if it is IT or finance? Give me a call when you can. Thanks.
